newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hashimoto uses dashing image to woo voters.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto uses dashing image to woo voters.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has emerged as his party's biggest electoral asset, using his personal charm to deflect attention from the Liberal Democratic Party's scandal-plagued past.
At appearances ahead of Sunday's general election, Hashimoto has turned on the tricks of a veteran campaigner, from the moment he gets out of his car to warm handshakes with supporters.
At the rail terminal at Izumi-Otsu, a suburb of Osaka in western Japan, the sound of rustling paper "Rising Sun" flags held by the crowd rose as his limousine neared.
"He's here! Ryu-chan!" normally restrained middle-aged women shout in the crowd.
Living up to his lively image, Hashimoto, 59, does not just get out of his car -- he jumps out. He does not stroll -- he jogs to the campaign van.
Atop a van, Hashimoto delivers his well-rehearsed speech of apology for things not done, the need for gradual reforms and calls for stability.
"We have indeed found it difficult to win back the trust we lost three years ago," he says.
He always starts out with this apology for the series of scandals that toppled his party from power in 1993.
"He's sooooooo handsome," says Kiku Oshima, a middle-aged housewife. "He looks a lot better than on TV."
Hashimoto has abandoned the garb of the traditional Japanese campaigner -- while gloves and a white sash emblazoned with his name and a huge rosette.
Instead, he wears a sharply cut dark-blue suit and his trademark slick hair completes an image some women find attractive.
Catching listeners' attention with his apology for LDP excesses, Hashimoto turns to the pressing need to restore full economic recovery.
Similarly important, he says, is a plan to introduce around-the-clock nursing for ailing senior citizens, the key programme in his party's welfare policies.
"I must now talk about something very tough. When I was handed the prime ministership, I again checked the country's debts and I was shocked. It is now 44 trillion yen ($392 billion)..."
Not mentioned is the fact that, as former finance and trade minister, Hashimoto has always been up-to-date on government finances.

He takes a stab at his closest rival, Ichiro Ozawa's opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), which has been campaigning on promises of an 18 trillion yen ($160 billion) income tax cut and a freeze on the sales tax.
But Hashimoto doesn't mention the opposition party or Ozawa by name.
He repeats the carefully constructed, 15-minute speech at other locations on his stumping tour, as many as 12 different places a day, mixing praise for candidates and issues peculiar to the locality.
"Sometimes, Mr Nakayama comes to me and scolds me outright. Now I need a man like (former foreign minister Taro) Nakayama," Hashimoto says.
